method_card.title: Concentration and Titration
steps: Convert every volume from cm³ to dm³ (divide by 1000).
Find moles of the substance you know: n = c × V.
Cross the balanced equation by its mole ratio to reach the unknown.
Divide moles by volume for the concentration, and state the unit.
method_card.content:
Concentration is how much solute sits in each dm³ of solution.

  • \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) gives mol/dm³
  • \(c_g = \dfrac{m}{V}\) gives g/dm³
  • \(n = \dfrac{m}{M_r}\) turns mass into moles

Volume must be in dm³, so divide any cm³ figure by 1000 first. In a titration, find the moles you know, cross the balanced equation by its mole ratio, then divide by the other volume. Average the concordant titres and discard the rough one.

exam_context.frequency: High: concentration and titration calculations appear in almost every Chemistry paper

gold.display: 5.3 g of Na₂CO₃ is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl. The titre is 25.0 cm³. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of HCl. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Mr Na₂CO₃ = (2×23) + 12 + (3×16) = 106. n = 5.3 ÷ 106 = 0.05 mol, c(flask) = 0.2 mol/dm³, sample n = 0.005 mol, ratio 1:2 gives n(HCl) = 0.01, c = 0.40 mol/dm³.
Na₂CO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2. Double the carbonate moles to get 0.01 mol HCl. Forgetting to double gives 0.005 ÷ 0.025 = 0.2.

gold.hint: Work down to the sample moles, apply the 1:2 ratio, then divide by the titre.

guided_steps.say: A five step chain: Mr, moles in the flask, flask concentration, moles in the sample, then the ratio and final concentration.

guided_steps.hint: n = c × V, sample volume 0.025 dm³.
c × V returns the HCl moles.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.01 mol HCl, matching the 1:2 ratio, so 0.40 mol/dm³ is right.

gold.display: A student dissolves KOH in water and makes up 500 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of this is titrated with 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ HCl. KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O. Calculate the mass of KOH originally dissolved. (Ar: K = 39, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: You titrated 25.0 cm³ from a 500 cm³ flask, so scale up: total mol = 0.08 × 0.5 = 0.04 mol, mass = 0.04 × 56 = 2.24 g. Skipping the scale-up gives only 0.112 g.
The 25.0 cm³ sample is one twentieth of the 500 cm³ flask. Multiply the concentration by 0.5 dm³ to get the total moles.

gold.hint: Find total moles in the flask, scale to 500 cm³, then multiply by the formula mass.

guided_steps.say: Work back from the titration to the original mass: acid moles, base moles, base concentration, scale to the whole flask, then mass.
Ratio KOH : HCl is 1 : 1, so moles of KOH in the 25.0 cm³ sample = 0.002 mol.

guided_steps.hint: c = n ÷ V, sample volume 0.025 dm³.

guided_steps.pre: Scale to the whole 500 cm³ flask (0.5 dm³): 0.08 × 0.5 =

guided_steps.hint: mass ÷ Mr returns the total moles.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.04 mol in the flask, so 2.24 g is right.

gold.display: Calculate the mass of HCl needed to make 500 cm³ of a 0.4 mol/dm³ solution. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)

misconceptions.message: Convert 500 cm³ to 0.5 dm³ first. n = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 mol, mass = 0.2 × 36.5 = 7.3 g. Using 500 gives 7300 g.
Mr HCl = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5, not 36. Mass = 0.2 × 36.5 = 7.3 g. Using 36 gives 7.2 g.

gold.hint: Moles from concentration and volume, then mass = moles × formula mass.

guided_steps.say: Moles first, then mass: \(n = c \times V\) then mass = \(n \times M_r\).

guided_steps.hint: Add Ar of H and Cl.

guided_steps.done: Returns 0.2 mol, so 7.3 g is right.

gold.display: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH is titrated with three concordant titres of 18.70, 18.65 and 18.75 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ HCl. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: Divide by the NaOH volume (0.025 dm³), not the titre. n(NaOH) = 0.00374 mol, so c = 0.00374 ÷ 0.025 = 0.1496 mol/dm³. Using 0.0187 gives 0.2.
Mean titre = 18.70 cm³ = 0.01870 dm³. n(HCl) = 0.003740 mol, c = 0.1496 mol/dm³, which rounds to 0.150 to 3 sig figs.
Average the three concordant results before using the titre: (18.70 + 18.65 + 18.75) ÷ 3 = 18.70 cm³.

gold.hint: Mean titre first, then moles, the 1:1 ratio, and the base concentration.

guided_steps.say: First the mean titre, then moles of acid, the 1 : 1 ratio, and the base concentration.

guided_steps.hint: Add the three and divide by 3.

guided_steps.say: Ratio 1 : 1, so moles of NaOH = 0.00374 mol.

guided_steps.done: 0.150 mol/dm³ to 3 sig figs, so the answer is right.

gold.display: A student makes up a standard solution of citric acid (Mr = 192) by dissolving 4.80 g in water and making up to 250 cm³. She titrates 25.0 cm³ of this against NaOH; the titre is 25.0 cm³. The equation is: H₃C₆H₅O₇ + 3NaOH → Na₃C₆H₅O₇ + 3H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: The equation shows 3 moles of NaOH per mole of citric acid. n(acid, sample) = 0.0025 mol, so n(NaOH) = 0.0075 mol and c = 0.0075 ÷ 0.025 = 0.30 mol/dm³. Forgetting to triple gives 0.1.
Three moles of NaOH react with one mole of citric acid. Multiply the acid moles by 3.

gold.hint: Acid concentration, then sample moles, the 1:3 ratio, then the titre volume.

guided_steps.say: Chain through: acid moles, acid concentration, sample moles, then the 1 : 3 ratio and final concentration.

guided_steps.pre: Moles of citric acid in the flask: 4.80 ÷ 192 =
Moles of acid in the 25.0 cm³ sample: 0.1 × 0.025 =

guided_steps.hint: c × V returns the NaOH moles.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.0075 mol NaOH, matching the 1:3 ratio, so 0.30 mol/dm³ is right.

gold.display: A student makes up a standard solution of citric acid (Mr = 192) by dissolving 4.80 g in water and making up to 250 cm³. She titrates 25.0 cm³ of this against NaOH; the titre is 30.0 cm³. The equation is: H₃C₆H₅O₇ + 3NaOH → Na₃C₆H₅O₇ + 3H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: n(acid, sample) = 0.0025 mol. Ratio 1 : 3, so n(NaOH) = 0.0075 mol and c = 0.0075 ÷ 0.030 = 0.25 mol/dm³. Forgetting to triple gives 0.0833.
Three moles of NaOH react with one mole of citric acid. Multiply the acid moles by 3.

gold.hint: Same chain as before but the titre is 30.0 cm³.

guided_steps.say: The same chain: acid moles, acid concentration, sample moles, ratio, final concentration.

guided_steps.pre: Moles of citric acid in the flask: 4.80 ÷ 192 =
Moles of acid in the 25.0 cm³ sample: 0.1 × 0.025 =

guided_steps.hint: Titre 30.0 cm³ = 0.030 dm³; c = n ÷ V.
c × V returns the NaOH moles.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.0075 mol NaOH, so 0.25 mol/dm³ is right.

bronze.display: Calculate the concentration (mol/dm³) of a solution containing 0.5 mol of solute in 250 cm³ of solution.
bronze.equation_hint: \(c = n \div V\) (convert cm³ to dm³ first)

misconceptions.message: Convert 250 cm³ to 0.25 dm³ first. Then c = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2.0 mol/dm³. Dividing by 250 gives 0.002, far too small.
Concentration = moles ÷ volume, not moles × volume. 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125 is the wrong way round.

bronze.hint: Convert cm³ to dm³, then divide moles by volume.

guided_steps.say: Concentration in mol/dm³ is \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\), and the volume must be in dm³.

guided_steps.done: That returns the 0.5 mol we started with, so 2.0 mol/dm³ is right.

bronze.display: How many moles are in 200 cm³ of a 0.25 mol/dm³ solution?

misconceptions.message: 200 cm³ = 0.2 dm³. n = 0.25 × 0.2 = 0.05 mol. Using 200 gives 50, a thousand times too big.

bronze.hint: Convert the volume to dm³, then multiply concentration by volume.

guided_steps.say: Moles from concentration and volume: \(n = c \times V\), volume in dm³.

guided_steps.hint: Dividing moles by volume returns the concentration.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.25 mol/dm³, so 0.05 mol is right.

bronze.display: What volume (in dm³) of a 0.4 mol/dm³ solution contains 0.06 mol?

misconceptions.message: Rearrange to V = n ÷ c = 0.06 ÷ 0.4 = 0.15 dm³. Dividing c by n (0.4 ÷ 0.06) is upside down.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) for volume: \(V = \dfrac{n}{c}\).

guided_steps.hint: c × V should give the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.06 mol, so the volume is 0.15 dm³.

bronze.display: 3.65 g of HCl is dissolved in water to make 500 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.

misconceptions.message: 500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³. c = 3.65 ÷ 0.5 = 7.3 g/dm³. Dividing by 500 gives 0.0073, far too small.

bronze.hint: For g/dm³ divide the mass by the volume in dm³.

guided_steps.say: For g/dm³ use mass directly: \(c_g = \dfrac{m}{V}\), no moles needed.

guided_steps.done: Returns 3.65 g, so 7.3 g/dm³ is right.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 4.0 g of NaOH. (Mr: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Mr of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40. Then n = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.1 mol.

bronze.hint: Add the Ar values for the formula mass, then divide the mass by it.

guided_steps.say: Moles from mass: \(n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\).

guided_steps.hint: Add the Ar values for Na, O and H.

guided_steps.done: Returns 4.0 g, so 0.1 mol is right.

bronze.display: A solution has a concentration of 0.3 mol/dm³. How many moles are in 100 cm³?

misconceptions.message: 100 cm³ = 0.1 dm³. n = 0.3 × 0.1 = 0.03 mol. Using 100 gives 30.

bronze.hint: Convert to dm³, then multiply concentration by volume.

guided_steps.say: Moles from concentration and volume: \(n = c \times V\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide moles by volume to check.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.3 mol/dm³, so 0.03 mol is right.

misconceptions.message: There are 1000 cm³ in a dm³, not 100. Divide by 1000: 750 ÷ 1000 = 0.75 dm³. Dividing by 100 gives 7.5, ten times too big.

bronze.hint: There are 1000 cm³ in a dm³, so divide by 1000.

guided_steps.say: There are 1000 cm³ in 1 dm³, so dividing by 1000 converts cm³ to dm³.

guided_steps.hint: Move the decimal point three places left.

guided_steps.done: Back to 750 cm³, so 0.75 dm³ is right.

bronze.display: Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³ of a solution made by dissolving 5.85 g of NaCl in 500 cm³ of water. (Ar: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
bronze.equation_hint: First find moles using \(n = m \div M_r\), then \(c = n \div V\)
bronze.hint: Find the formula mass, then moles, then divide by the volume in dm³.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: mass to moles with \(n = \dfrac{m}{M_r}\), then \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\).

guided_steps.hint: Add the Ar values for Na and Cl.

guided_steps.done: Returns 0.1 mol, so 0.2 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of HCl of unknown concentration is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ NaOH. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) → mole ratio → \(c = n \div V\)

misconceptions.message: Keep both volumes in dm³. n(NaOH) = 0.150 × 0.020 = 0.003 mol, then c(HCl) = 0.003 ÷ 0.025 = 0.12 mol/dm³.
Divide by the HCl volume (0.025 dm³) in the last step, not the NaOH volume. Using 0.020 gives 0.15, which is wrong.

silver.hint: Find moles of NaOH, use the 1:1 ratio, then divide by the HCl volume.

guided_steps.say: Titration order: moles you know, then mole ratio, then the unknown concentration.
The ratio HCl : NaOH is 1 : 1, so the moles of HCl are the same: 0.003 mol.

guided_steps.hint: c = n ÷ V, using the HCl volume.
c × V returns the moles of HCl.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.003 mol HCl, matching the 1:1 ratio, so 0.12 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ Ca(OH)₂ is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of HCl. Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl.
silver.equation_hint: Apply the 1:2 mole ratio for Ca(OH)₂ : HCl

misconceptions.message: The ratio is 1 : 2. n(Ca(OH)₂) = 0.0025 mol, so n(HCl) = 0.005 mol and c = 0.005 ÷ 0.020 = 0.25 mol/dm³. Forgetting to double gives 0.125.
Two moles of HCl react with every one mole of Ca(OH)₂. Double the moles before finding concentration.

silver.hint: Double the calcium hydroxide moles for the 1:2 ratio before finding concentration.

guided_steps.say: Find moles of the calcium hydroxide, apply the 1 : 2 ratio, then divide by the acid volume.

guided_steps.pre: Ratio is 1 : 2, so moles of HCl: 0.0025 × 2 =
guided_steps.hint: Two HCl per Ca(OH)₂, so double.
c × V returns the HCl moles.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.005 mol HCl, so 0.25 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄ is titrated against NaOH. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. The titre is 25.0 cm³. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH.
silver.equation_hint: H₂SO₄ : NaOH = 1 : 2, so double the moles of H₂SO₄

misconceptions.message: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.20 × 0.025 = 0.005 mol. NaOH needs double: 0.010 mol, so c = 0.010 ÷ 0.025 = 0.40 mol/dm³. Forgetting to double gives 0.2.
Two moles of NaOH react with every one mole of H₂SO₄. Multiply the acid moles by 2.

silver.hint: Double the acid moles for the 1:2 ratio to get NaOH moles.

guided_steps.say: Moles of acid, then double for NaOH (1 : 2), then divide by the NaOH volume.

guided_steps.hint: c × V returns the NaOH moles.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.01 mol NaOH, so 0.40 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: A student carries out three titrations with concordant results of 24.80 cm³, 24.85 cm³ and 24.75 cm³. A rough titre of 25.30 cm³ was also recorded. Calculate the mean titre to use.
silver.equation_hint: Mean of the three concordant results (within 0.10 cm³ of each other). Exclude the rough titre.

misconceptions.message: The rough titre (25.30 cm³) is discarded. Mean = (24.80 + 24.85 + 24.75) ÷ 3 = 24.80 cm³. Including the rough gives 24.925.
Keep two decimal places for burette readings to match the precision of the equipment.

silver.hint: Average only the three concordant titres and discard the rough one.

guided_steps.say: Only concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³ of each other) go into the mean. The rough titre is discarded.

guided_steps.hint: Add only the three close values.
Largest minus smallest of the three.
guided_steps.done: The three agree within 0.10 cm³, so the mean 24.80 cm³ is valid.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.08 mol/dm³ KOH is neutralised by HNO₃. KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O. The titre is 20.0 cm³. Calculate the concentration of the HNO₃.
silver.equation_hint: 1:1 ratio. \(n = c \times V\) then \(c = n \div V\)

misconceptions.message: Divide by the HNO₃ volume (0.020 dm³) in the last step. n(KOH) = 0.08 × 0.025 = 0.002 mol, so c = 0.002 ÷ 0.020 = 0.10 mol/dm³. Using the KOH volume gives 0.08.

silver.hint: 1:1 ratio, so use the KOH moles as the acid moles, then the acid volume.

guided_steps.say: 1 : 1 ratio, so moles of acid equal moles of base. Find KOH moles, then divide by the acid volume.
Ratio 1 : 1, so moles of HNO₃ = 0.002 mol.

guided_steps.hint: c × V returns the acid moles.
guided_steps.done: Returns 0.002 mol, so 0.10 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: Calculate the concentration in g/dm³ of a solution made by dissolving 10.6 g of Na₂CO₃ in 200 cm³ of water. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
silver.equation_hint: \(c_g = m \div V\) (V in dm³). No need to find moles for g/dm³.

misconceptions.message: 200 cm³ = 0.2 dm³. c = 10.6 ÷ 0.2 = 53.0 g/dm³. Dividing by 200 gives 0.053.

silver.hint: For g/dm³ divide mass by the volume in dm³, no moles needed.

guided_steps.say: g/dm³ uses mass straight away: \(c_g = \dfrac{m}{V}\).

guided_steps.done: Returns 10.6 g, so 53.0 g/dm³ is right.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One concentration formula, units fixed first, then a single divide or multiply
problem_bank.silver_description: A titration: moles of the known, the mole ratio, then the unknown concentration
problem_bank.gold_description: A multi-step chain: mass to moles or flask scaling, plus a non 1:1 ratio

worked_examples.question: 4.0 g of NaOH (Mr = 40) is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against H₂SO₄. The titre is 12.5 cm³. The equation is: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the H₂SO₄ in mol/dm³.

bronze.title: Bronze: one formula, one divide
steps: A concentration question gives you two of the three parts of \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) and asks for the third.
First fix the units: volume must be in dm³, so divide any cm³ figure by 1000.
Then substitute and do the single divide or multiply. State mol/dm³ or g/dm³.

example.question: Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³ of 0.5 mol in 250 cm³.

silver.title: Silver: titration in three moves
steps: You know the concentration and volume of one solution and one volume of the other. Find the moles you can: \(n = c \times V\).
Cross the balanced equation by its mole ratio to get the moles of the unknown.
Divide those moles by the unknown's volume (in dm³) for its concentration.

example.question: 25.0 cm³ of HCl is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ NaOH (1:1). Find the HCl concentration.

gold.title: Gold: the full chain
steps: Extra links appear: mass to moles with \(n = \dfrac{m}{M_r}\), or scaling between a titrated sample and the whole flask.
Build the chain in order and keep every volume in dm³. A non 1 : 1 ratio means multiply or divide by that ratio.
Finish with the quantity asked for, then check by working backwards.

example.question: 5.3 g Na₂CO₃ made to 250 cm³; 25.0 cm³ needs 25.0 cm³ HCl (1:2). Find the HCl concentration.

opener.label: Before any formula
opener.display: 8 g of salt is stirred into 2 litres of water.

steps.pre: Grams of salt in each litre =
steps.say: No formula needed, just share it out. If 8 g of salt is spread evenly through 2 litres, each litre holds an equal share.

steps.pre: Grams of salt in each litre now =
steps.say: Now tip the same 8 g into 4 litres instead. Same salt, more water.

That share per litre is concentration: amount ÷ volume. More water with the same salt makes it weaker. Chemistry writes it \(c_g = \dfrac{m}{V}\) in g/dm³, or \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) in mol/dm³. A dm³ is just a litre.

bronze.display: Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³ of 0.6 mol dissolved in 300 cm³.
bronze.label: Together: your first one

steps.say: Bronze concentration: one formula, \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\), volume in dm³.

steps.done: Back to 0.6 mol, so 2.0 mol/dm³ is right. Bronze is just this one divide.

silver.display: 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ NaOH is neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of HCl. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl.
silver.label: Together: the silver move

steps.say: Silver adds the titration order: moles of the known, mole ratio, then the unknown concentration.
Ratio NaOH : HCl is 1 : 1, so moles of HCl = 0.002 mol.

steps.done: Returns 0.002 mol, so 0.080 mol/dm³ is right.

gold.display: 1.60 g of NaOH (Mr = 40) is dissolved and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ is titrated with 0.20 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄. 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the volume of H₂SO₄ needed.
gold.label: Together: the gold move

steps.say: Gold chains it all: mass to moles, flask concentration, sample moles, the 2 : 1 ratio, then rearrange for volume.

steps.pre: Moles of NaOH in the flask: 1.60 ÷ 40 =
Moles of NaOH in the 25.0 cm³ sample: 0.16 × 0.025 =

steps.hint: Two NaOH per acid, so halve.

steps.done: 10 cm³ of H₂SO₄, so the answer is right.
